warmup.q: An NIO server (one built on java.nio, Java's non-blocking IO package) registers every connection for OP_READ | OP_WRITE, asking to hear whenever a connection can be read or written, so it can write "whenever it needs to". One client connects and sends nothing. What does the server's loop do for the next second?
options: Sleeps in select() until the client sends something
Wakes once, sees nothing to write, and goes back to sleep
Wakes up again and again, hundreds of thousands of times, because the socket is always writable
warmup.why: A socket with free space in its send buffer counts as writable, and on Linux the selector reports a ready socket on every check for as long as it stays ready, like a light that stays on. So every select() returns at once. The demo in this lesson counted 0 wakeups with OP_READ alone and 374,510 in 300 ms with OP_WRITE added.

opening:
Last lesson's post office gave every customer a clerk. Picture it rebuilt. Each customer now gets a box in the wall, with a small light above it. A customer drops a form through the slot whenever it's ready, and the light comes on. Behind the wall sits one clerk, who looks at the lights, serves only the boxes that are lit, and dozes when none are.

That's the plan Blocking IO, threads and the C10K problem ended on, and Java has shipped the parts since Java 1.4: buffers, channels and a selector. Build the echo server on them, and it passes a quick test. Then, under load, it quietly loses bytes, with no exception at all. Leave it idle overnight, and one core runs at 100% while nobody sends a thing.

Both bugs come from small details that look harmless, which is why nearly everyone writes them once. In this lesson, we'll fill a buffer by hand, send bytes that don't all fit, wire up a selector, and switch off the light that never goes out. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We rebuilt the post office around a wall of lights: one thread, a selector, and a tray behind every box. The echo server now keeps the bytes a write couldn't send, crosses every key off its list, closes only when nothing is pending, and asks for the "room for a reply" light only while a reply is waiting.

Now search any selector loop you can find, in your own code or a library's, for OP_WRITE. Then find the line that turns it off again. If there isn't one, that loop spins.

Next, we'll hand this loop to Netty. Which of today's rules does a library follow for you, and which one can it never follow on your behalf?

sections.h: The tray behind each box: a ByteBuffer's position and limit
sections.html:
Start with the tray. Everything in java.nio, Java's package for non-blocking input and output, moves bytes through a ByteBuffer. In the post office, it's the tray behind each box: a fixed number of slots, a cursor that marks the next slot to fill or empty, and a stop line.

In Java, those are three numbers. capacity is the tray's size. position is the cursor: where the next put or get happens. limit is the stop line: where reading or writing must stop. Most NIO bugs are one of these three numbers being wrong.

A fresh buffer is ready for filling, which we'll call write mode: position at 0 and limit at capacity. Each put moves position forward. Before you can read what you wrote, flip() draws the stop line where filling ended (limit becomes position) and moves the cursor back to the start (position becomes 0). BufferDemo, in the Try it below, walks a 16-byte buffer through the whole cycle:

allocate(16)         pos=0  lim=16 cap=16 remaining=16
put("hello")         pos=5  lim=16 cap=16 remaining=11
flip()               pos=0  lim=5  cap=16 remaining=5
get(2) -> "he"       pos=2  lim=5  cap=16 remaining=3
compact()            pos=3  lim=16 cap=16 remaining=13
put("XY")            pos=5  lim=16 cap=16 remaining=11
flip()               pos=0  lim=5  cap=16 remaining=5
readable content: "lloXY"

After get(2) took he, where should new bytes go? compact() answers that. It slides the unread bytes (llo) to the front of the tray and puts the buffer back in write mode right after them, so new data lands behind what you haven't used yet. That's why the content ends as lloXY. clear() looks similar and does something else: it resets both marks and forgets everything, read or not.

Forget flip() and nothing complains. A buffer of 8 with 2 bytes put has remaining() 6, so a write sends the 6 bytes after your data, whatever happens to sit in those slots. The buffer will hand over garbage without a murmur, as long as the numbers say so.

There are two kinds of buffer. allocate gives a heap buffer, backed by a byte[] on the Java heap, the memory where Java keeps its objects. allocateDirect gives memory outside the heap. The kernel, the core of the operating system, reads and writes memory by address during a system call (a request a program makes to the kernel), and the garbage collector is allowed to move a byte[] around. So the JDK copies a heap buffer through a temporary direct buffer on every channel read and write (sun.nio.ch.IOUtil does it).

Direct buffers skip that copy, but the ByteBuffer Javadoc says they have "somewhat higher allocation and deallocation costs" and recommends them for large, long-lived buffers. So allocate direct buffers once and reuse them. Netty's allocators, lesson 4, do exactly that.

A buffer's mode lives in two numbers the compiler can't see. Flip before you read, and compact to keep what's unread.

A tray is only half the story. The other half is what the kernel does with it.

code.title: BufferDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.nio.l02; import java.nio.ByteBuffer; import static java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets.US_ASCII; /** Walks a ByteBuffer through put, flip, get, compact and clear, printing its cursor after each step. */ public class BufferDemo { static void show(String step, ByteBuffer b) { System.out.printf("%-20s pos=%-2d lim=%-2d cap=%-2d remaining=%d%n", step, b.position(), b.limit(), b.capacity(), b.remaining()); } public static void main(String[] args) { ByteBuffer b = ByteBuffer.allocate(16); show("allocate(16)", b); b.put("hello".getBytes(US_ASCII)); show("put(\"hello\")", b); b.flip(); // write mode -> read mode: limit = position, position = 0 show("flip()", b); byte[] two = new byte[2]; b.get(two); show("get(2) -> \"" + new String(two, US_ASCII) + "\"", b); b.compact(); // move the unread "llo" to the front, back to write mode show("compact()", b); b.put("XY".getBytes(US_ASCII)); show("put(\"XY\")", b); b.flip(); show("flip()", b); byte[] rest = new byte[b.remaining()]; b.get(rest); System.out.println("readable content: \"" + new String(rest, US_ASCII) + "\""); ByteBuffer forgot = ByteBuffer.allocate(8); forgot.put((byte) 1).put((byte) 2); // no flip() before handing it to write() System.out.println("forgot flip(): remaining()=" + forgot.remaining() + ", so a write would send 6 stale bytes, not the 2 you put"); ByteBuffer heap = ByteBuffer.allocate(64), direct = ByteBuffer.allocateDirect(64); System.out.println("heap: isDirect=" + heap.isDirect() + " hasArray=" + heap.hasArray() + " " + heap.getClass().getName()); System.out.println("direct: isDirect=" + direct.isDirect() + " hasArray=" + direct.hasArray() + " " + direct.getClass().getName()); } }

sections.h: Non-blocking reads and writes move only what fits
sections.html:
A socket is a program's handle on one end of a network connection, and TCP is the protocol that carries its bytes in order. Every TCP socket has two buffers inside the kernel. The receive buffer holds bytes that arrived from the network and that your program hasn't read yet. The send buffer holds bytes your program wrote that the kernel hasn't delivered yet. In the post office, they're the box's street-side slot and its pick-up shelf: letters waiting to come in, and replies waiting to be collected.

read and write never touch the network themselves. They copy between your ByteBuffer and these two kernel buffers.

A channel is java.nio's handle on something bytes move through, such as a socket or a file. Put a SocketChannel in non-blocking mode with configureBlocking(false), and its copies stop waiting. They do what the kernel buffers allow right now, and return.

read(buf) copies whatever sits in the receive buffer. That can be one byte, half a line, three lines, or nothing at all, in which case it returns 0. It returns -1 when the other side has closed its end.

write(buf) is the call that bites. Its Javadoc says a socket channel in non-blocking mode "cannot write any more bytes than are free in the socket's output buffer". When the client reads slowly, the send buffer fills up, and write sends part of your buffer, or none of it. That's a partial write, a reply that only half fits on the shelf.

So every connection needs its own buffer for the bytes it hasn't sent yet. The pattern that handles both directions is four lines:

Java
int n = ch.read(buf);    // append whatever arrived, maybe 0 bytes; -1 means the client is done
buf.flip();              // switch to reading what we hold
ch.write(buf);           // send what the kernel accepts, maybe only part of it
buf.compact();           // keep the unsent tail at the front, back to write mode
Kotlin
val n = ch.read(buf)     // append whatever arrived, maybe 0 bytes; -1 means the client is done
buf.flip()               // switch to reading what we hold
ch.write(buf)            // send what the kernel accepts, maybe only part of it
buf.compact()            // keep the unsent tail at the front, back to write mode

First we read, appending to whatever the tray already holds. Then we flip, write what the kernel takes, and compact, so the unsent tail moves to the front. After compact(), buf.position() > 0 means bytes are still waiting to go. One run for this track echoed 8 MiB to a client with a 4 KiB receive buffer and counted 8 partial writes. With clear() in place of compact(), each of them would have dropped bytes.

The read side has a twin rule: one read is not one message. TCP is a byte stream. A line sent with one write can arrive in three reads, and two lines can arrive in one. Here the post office picture breaks. A real letter arrives whole, but bytes arrive in whatever pieces the network made. Anything beyond a raw echo needs framing, a way to tell where one message ends, such as a newline at the end or a length at the front. Lessons 3 and 4 let Netty do it.

One trap lives in the client, too. If a test client writes 8 MiB and only then starts reading, the echo stalls. The server can't send because the client isn't reading, so the server stops reading, so the client's write blocks. Clients of an echo server must read and write at the same time, and the lab's tests use a writer thread for exactly that reason.

Non-blocking calls move only what fits. Keep the rest per connection, and frame what you read.

We can read and write without waiting now. What's missing is someone to tell the clerk which boxes to look at.

The idle test fails too, with a wakeup count in the hundreds of thousands.

sections.h: The wall of lights: a Selector tells one thread which channels are ready
sections.html:
A Selector is the wall of lights. It watches many channels at once. You register each channel with an interest set, the events you want to hear about: OP_ACCEPT (a new client is waiting), OP_READ (bytes arrived) and OP_WRITE (there's room to send). Then select() blocks until at least one of them is ready.

Each registration is a SelectionKey. It carries the interest set, the ready set that the selector fills in, and an attachment, a slot where you keep that connection's state, like a card pinned to the box. Here is the clerk's day:

Java
while (true) {
    selector.select();                                  // sleep until something is ready
    Iterator<SelectionKey> it = selector.selectedKeys().iterator();
    while (it.hasNext()) {
        SelectionKey key = it.next();
        it.remove();                                    // you must remove handled keys yourself
        if (key.isAcceptable()) {
            SocketChannel ch = server.accept();
            ch.configureBlocking(false);
            ch.register(selector, SelectionKey.OP_READ, new Conn());
        } else {
            serve(key);                                 // read, write, update the interest set
        }
    }
}
Kotlin
while (true) {
    selector.select()                                   // sleep until something is ready
    val it = selector.selectedKeys().iterator()
    while (it.hasNext()) {
        val key = it.next()
        it.remove()                                     // you must remove handled keys yourself
        if (key.isAcceptable) {
            val ch = server.accept()
            ch.configureBlocking(false)
            ch.register(selector, SelectionKey.OP_READ, Conn())
        } else {
            serve(key)                                  // read, write, update the interest set
        }
    }
}

First, select() sleeps until a light comes on. Then we walk the list of lit boxes, selectedKeys(). A lit accept key means a new customer, so we accept the channel, make it non-blocking and give it a box of its own, with a fresh Conn card. Any other key is a box with something to do, and serve handles it.

The it.remove() line looks like housekeeping, and it isn't. The selector adds keys to the selected set and never takes them out. Leave a key in, and the next pass handles it again, with its old ready set. It's a list of lit boxes that nobody crosses off. StaleKeyDemo, in the Try it below, sends exactly one 6-byte message and loops for 300 ms:

remove handled keys=true  loops=7, handled as readable 1 times, bytes read 6
remove handled keys=false loops=7, handled as readable 7 times, bytes read 6

Seven visits to a box that held one letter. For an accept key, the same mistake means calling accept() again and getting null back.

The selector comes with a threading rule, too. Its Javadoc says a selector is safe for use by several threads, but its selected-key set is not. The simple way to obey that is the one every library uses: one thread, one path of work through the program, owns a selector, runs its loop, and does all the work for its channels. Netty, in the next lesson, calls that thread an event loop.

On Linux, Selector.open() returns sun.nio.ch.EPollSelectorImpl, a wrapper around epoll, the Linux system call from lesson 1 that reports ready sockets. On macOS you get a kqueue selector. The JDK registers sockets with epoll in level-triggered mode: as long as a socket is readable or writable, every select() reports it again, like a light that stays on while there's mail in the box. The other mode, edge-triggered, is more like a bell that rings once when a letter arrives. A light that stays on is forgiving for reads. For writes, it's the bug in the next section.

The selector never crosses a box off your list. Remove every key you handle.

try.title: Forget it.remove()
steps: Open StaleKeyDemo.java (or StaleKeyDemo.kt). A client sends exactly one 6-byte message, and the loop runs for 300 ms, once removing handled keys and once not.
Predict how many times each version treats the channel as readable.
Run it with the command below.

code.title: StaleKeyDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.nio.l02; import java.net.InetAddress; import java.net.InetSocketAddress; import java.nio.ByteBuffer; import java.nio.channels.SelectionKey; import java.nio.channels.Selector; import java.nio.channels.ServerSocketChannel; import java.nio.channels.SocketChannel; import java.util.Iterator; /** One message arrives. How many times does the loop think the channel is readable? */ public class StaleKeyDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { run(true); run(false); } static void run(boolean removeHandledKeys) throws Exception { try (Selector selector = Selector.open(); ServerSocketChannel server = ServerSocketChannel.open()) { server.bind(new InetSocketAddress(InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress(), 0)); try (SocketChannel client = SocketChannel.open(server.getLocalAddress()); SocketChannel conn = server.accept()) { conn.configureBlocking(false); conn.register(selector, SelectionKey.OP_READ); client.write(ByteBuffer.wrap("letter".getBytes())); // exactly one message ByteBuffer buf = ByteBuffer.allocate(64); int loops = 0, handled = 0, bytes = 0; long end = System.nanoTime() + 300_000_000L; while (System.nanoTime() < end) { selector.select(50); loops++; Iterator<SelectionKey> it = selector.selectedKeys().iterator(); while (it.hasNext()) { SelectionKey key = it.next(); if (removeHandledKeys) it.remove(); if (key.isReadable()) { // ready set from the last select that added the key handled++; buf.clear(); bytes += Math.max(0, conn.read(buf)); } } } System.out.printf("remove handled keys=%-5s loops=%d, handled as readable %d times, bytes read %d%n", removeHandledKeys, loops, handled, bytes); } } } }

How many times does the loop think the channel is readable? */ fun main() { staleKeys(removeHandledKeys = true) staleKeys(removeHandledKeys = false) } private fun staleKeys(removeHandledKeys: Boolean) { Selector.open().use { selector -> ServerSocketChannel.open().use { server -> server.bind(InetSocketAddress(InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress(), 0)) SocketChannel.open(server.localAddress).use { client -> server.accept().use { conn -> conn.configureBlocking(false) conn.register(selector, SelectionKey.OP_READ) client.write(ByteBuffer.wrap("letter".toByteArray())) // exactly one message val buf = ByteBuffer.allocate(64) var loops = 0 var handled = 0 var bytes = 0 val end = System.nanoTime() + 300_000_000L while (System.nanoTime() < end) { selector.select(50) loops++ val it = selector.selectedKeys().iterator() while (it.hasNext()) { val key = it.next() if (removeHandledKeys) it.remove() if (key.isReadable) { // ready set from the last select that added the key handled++ buf.clear() bytes += maxOf(0, conn.read(buf)) } } } println("remove handled keys=%-5s loops=%d, handled as readable %d times, bytes read %d" .format(removeHandledKeys, loops, handled, bytes)) } } } } }

try.expect: With it.remove(): handled once, 6 bytes read. Without it: handled 7 times in 7 loop passes, still 6 bytes in total. The six extra passes each called read and got 0 bytes back, because the key stayed in the selected set and isReadable() kept answering from the old ready set.

sections.h: The light that never goes out: arm OP_WRITE only while bytes wait
sections.html:
A socket is writable whenever its send buffer has free space, which is nearly always. Put that next to a level-triggered selector, and you get the classic NIO bug. Register OP_WRITE on every connection, and its "room for a reply" light never goes out. select() returns at once, reports every idle connection as writable, and the loop goes around again.

SpinDemo measures it on one idle connection for 300 ms. One run on a busy 4-core machine printed:

Selector implementation: sun.nio.ch.EPollSelectorImpl
idle 300 ms, interest OP_READ           : 0 wakeups
idle 300 ms, interest OP_READ | OP_WRITE: 374510 wakeups

Zero against 374,510, on a connection that sent nothing. That's the clerk walking to a box, finding room for a reply nobody wrote, and walking back, more than a thousand times a millisecond. Under strace, a Linux tool that lists a program's system calls, the shape is just as clear: thousands of epoll_wait calls and a handful of epoll_ctl. On a real server, it shows up as one core at 100% with no traffic at all.

The fix is to register OP_READ by default and add OP_WRITE only while the connection has unsent bytes. When a write leaves bytes behind, arm it. When a later write drains them, drop it:

Java
boolean pending = conn.buf.position() > 0;   // after compact(): unsent bytes at the front
int ops = 0;
if (!conn.eof && conn.buf.hasRemaining()) ops |= SelectionKey.OP_READ;   // room left: keep reading
if (pending) ops |= SelectionKey.OP_WRITE;                                // only while bytes wait
key.interestOps(ops);
Kotlin
val pending = conn.buf.position() > 0        // after compact(): unsent bytes at the front
var ops = 0
if (!conn.eof && conn.buf.hasRemaining()) ops = ops or SelectionKey.OP_READ   // room left: keep reading
if (pending) ops = ops or SelectionKey.OP_WRITE                                // only while bytes wait
key.interestOps(ops)

The OP_READ line is the other half of the same idea. When the tray is full because the client reads slowly, stop reading from that client. Its bytes pile up in the kernel's receive buffer, and TCP tells the client how much room is left there (the TCP window). As the window shrinks to zero, the client's own writes stop. That's backpressure, a slow receiver slowing the sender down, in two lines. Lesson 4 shows Netty's version of it. In the 8 MiB run from earlier, the server armed OP_WRITE only 4 times in 537 selects.

Closing follows the same logic. A client can half-close a connection with shutdownOutput(): it says it will send nothing more, but it keeps reading. Your read then returns -1, the end-of-stream mark (EOF, short for end of file), yet the client still wants the rest of its echo. Close only once nothing is pending.

A writable socket is the normal case, not news. Ask for OP_WRITE only while bytes are waiting.

try.title: Watch the spin
steps: Run SpinDemo (or SpinDemoKt) with the command below. Predict both numbers first.
On Linux with strace installed, run it outside Gradle to count system calls: strace -f -c -e trace=epoll_wait,epoll_ctl java -cp nio/build/classes/java/demo workbench.nio.l02.SpinDemo.

code.title: SpinDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.nio.l02; import java.net.InetAddress; import java.net.InetSocketAddress; import java.nio.channels.SelectionKey; import java.nio.channels.Selector; import java.nio.channels.ServerSocketChannel; import java.nio.channels.SocketChannel; /** Counts how often select() wakes up on one idle connection, with and without OP_WRITE in the interest set. */ public class SpinDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { try (Selector probe = Selector.open()) { System.out.println("Selector implementation: " + probe.getClass().getName()); } System.out.println("idle 300 ms, interest OP_READ : " + wakeups(SelectionKey.OP_READ) + " wakeups"); System.out.println("idle 300 ms, interest OP_READ | OP_WRITE: " + wakeups(SelectionKey.OP_READ | SelectionKey.OP_WRITE) + " wakeups"); } static long wakeups(int interest) throws Exception { try (Selector selector = Selector.open(); ServerSocketChannel server = ServerSocketChannel.open()) { server.bind(new InetSocketAddress(InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress(), 0)); try (SocketChannel client = SocketChannel.open(server.getLocalAddress()); SocketChannel conn = server.accept()) { conn.configureBlocking(false); conn.register(selector, interest); long end = System.nanoTime() + 300_000_000L, count = 0; while (System.nanoTime() < end) { if (selector.select(50) > 0) count++; // nobody sends anything on this connection selector.selectedKeys().clear(); } return count; } } } }

alt.title: SpinDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.nio.l02 import java.net.InetAddress import java.net.InetSocketAddress import java.nio.channels.SelectionKey import java.nio.channels.Selector import java.nio.channels.ServerSocketChannel import java.nio.channels.SocketChannel /** Counts how often select() wakes up on one idle connection, with and without OP_WRITE in the interest set. */ fun main() { Selector.open().use { println("Selector implementation: ${it.javaClass.name}") } println("idle 300 ms, interest OP_READ : ${idleWakeups(SelectionKey.OP_READ)} wakeups") println("idle 300 ms, interest OP_READ | OP_WRITE: ${idleWakeups(SelectionKey.OP_READ or SelectionKey.OP_WRITE)} wakeups") } private fun idleWakeups(interest: Int): Long = Selector.open().use { selector -> ServerSocketChannel.open().use { server -> server.bind(InetSocketAddress(InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress(), 0)) SocketChannel.open(server.localAddress).use { _ -> server.accept().use { conn -> conn.configureBlocking(false) conn.register(selector, interest) val end = System.nanoTime() + 300_000_000L var count = 0L while (System.nanoTime() < end) { if (selector.select(50) > 0) count++ // nobody sends anything on this connection selector.selectedKeys().clear() } count } } } }

try.expect: 0 wakeups with OP_READ, and hundreds of thousands with OP_WRITE added (374,510 and 421,702 for the Java and Kotlin versions on a busy 4-core Linux machine; the exact number depends on processor speed and load). Under strace the loop slows down a lot, because strace stops the program on every system call, but the table still shows thousands of epoll_wait calls (4,315 in one run) against 5 epoll_ctl. On macOS the first line names the kqueue selector.

compare.title: The serve step in Java and Kotlin

java.title: serve, Java
java.html: private void serve(SelectionKey key) throws IOException { SocketChannel ch = (SocketChannel) key.channel(); Conn conn = (Conn) key.attachment(); if (key.isReadable() && ch.read(conn.buf) < 0) conn.eof = true; conn.buf.flip(); if (conn.buf.hasRemaining()) ch.write(conn.buf); conn.buf.compact(); boolean pending = conn.buf.position() > 0; if (conn.eof && !pending) { ch.close(); return; } int ops = 0; if (!conn.eof && conn.buf.hasRemaining()) ops |= SelectionKey.OP_READ; if (pending) ops |= SelectionKey.OP_WRITE; key.interestOps(ops); }

kotlin.title: serve, Kotlin
kotlin.html: private fun serve(key: SelectionKey) { val ch = key.channel() as SocketChannel val conn = key.attachment() as Conn if (key.isReadable && ch.read(conn.buf) < 0) conn.eof = true conn.buf.flip() if (conn.buf.hasRemaining()) ch.write(conn.buf) conn.buf.compact() val pending = conn.buf.position() > 0 if (conn.eof && !pending) { ch.close(); return } var ops = 0 if (!conn.eof && conn.buf.hasRemaining()) ops = ops or SelectionKey.OP_READ if (pending) ops = ops or SelectionKey.OP_WRITE key.interestOps(ops) }

compare.note: Both call the same JDK classes, so they behave the same: same partial writes, same level-triggered selector. The differences are on the surface, and they still trip people up. Kotlin has no |= for bit flags, so you write ops = ops or SelectionKey.OP_READ. Kotlin reads isReadable() and isAcceptable() as properties (key.isReadable), and the attachment is an untyped Any? that you cast with as Conn, just as Java casts from Object. Neither language helps with the buffer's mode: flip() and compact() change numbers at run time, not types, so neither compiler can stop you from writing a buffer that is still in write mode.

worked.title: Trace one connection through a partial write

steps.say: The client sends 20 KiB and reads slowly. The server's tray holds 16 KiB. First select(): readable. The server reads 16 KiB, flips, and the kernel accepts only 6 KiB of the write.
steps.code:
read 16384      -> pos=16384 lim=16384   (buffer full)
flip()          -> pos=0     lim=16384
write -> 6144   -> pos=6144  lim=16384   (10240 bytes not sent)
compact()       -> pos=10240 lim=16384   (pending: 10240, room: 6144)
interest        =  OP_READ | OP_WRITE

steps.say: Second select(): readable (the other 4 KiB arrived) and writable (the client read some). The server appends 4 KiB behind the pending bytes, then sends everything it holds.
steps.code:
read 4096       -> pos=14336 lim=16384
flip()          -> pos=0     lim=14336
write -> 14336  -> pos=14336 lim=14336   (all sent)
compact()       -> pos=0     lim=16384   (pending: 0)
interest        =  OP_READ               (OP_WRITE dropped: nothing to send)

steps.say: Now the client half-closes while the server still holds bytes. read returns -1, so stop reading, but keep OP_WRITE until the tail is gone. Close in the pass where pending reaches zero.
steps.code: // 1. remember EOF, don't close yet if (key.isReadable() && ch.read(conn.buf) < 0) conn.eof = true; // 2. send what we can, keep the rest conn.buf.flip(); if (conn.buf.hasRemaining()) ch.write(conn.buf); conn.buf.compact(); // 3. close only when drained; otherwise ask for exactly what we need boolean pending = conn.buf.position() > 0; if (conn.eof && !pending) { ch.close(); return; } key.interestOps((conn.eof ? 0 : SelectionKey.OP_READ) | (pending ? SelectionKey.OP_WRITE : 0));

alt.html: // 1. remember EOF, don't close yet if (key.isReadable && ch.read(conn.buf) < 0) conn.eof = true // 2. send what we can, keep the rest conn.buf.flip() if (conn.buf.hasRemaining()) ch.write(conn.buf) conn.buf.compact() // 3. close only when drained; otherwise ask for exactly what we need val pending = conn.buf.position() > 0 if (conn.eof && !pending) { ch.close(); return } key.interestOps((if (conn.eof) 0 else SelectionKey.OP_READ) or (if (pending) SelectionKey.OP_WRITE else 0))

steps.say: The lab's version adds one more condition: drop OP_READ while the tray has no room left. Without it, a full tray and a readable socket make the same spin as a stray OP_WRITE: select() says readable, read() copies 0 bytes into the full buffer, and the loop goes around again.

lab.title: Fix an NIO echo server that loses bytes and burns a core
steps: Run the tests. All three fail: the 4 MiB echo comes back short, the half-close test loses its tail, and an idle connection wakes the selector hundreds of thousands of times.
In accept(), register the new channel for OP_READ only.
In serve(), replace clear() with compact() so unsent bytes stay at the front, and only call write when the flipped buffer hasRemaining().
Close the channel only when conn.eof is true and nothing is pending (buf.position() == 0 after compact()).
End serve() by setting the interest set: OP_READ while not at EOF and the buffer has room, OP_WRITE only while bytes are pending. Run the tests three times.
hints: After compact(), position() is exactly the number of bytes still waiting to be sent.
The tests give the client a 4 KiB receive buffer, and the server's sockets an 8 KiB send buffer, so partial writes happen early and often. Your code must not depend on those sizes.
If idleConnectionDoesNotSpin still fails, look for any path through serve() that returns with OP_WRITE still set after the buffer drained.
The half-close test reads slowly on purpose. If it fails with a few kilobytes missing, you close on EOF before the pending bytes are written.
lab.done: All three tests in NioEchoServerTest pass, three runs in a row.

drill.title: Write the serve step from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. Write serve(SelectionKey key) for an echo server whose per-connection state is a ByteBuffer buf and a boolean eof: read, flip, write, compact, close on EOF only when drained, and set the interest ops. Then check: which line stops the busy spin, and which one applies backpressure?

answer.html: private void serve(SelectionKey key) throws IOException { SocketChannel ch = (SocketChannel) key.channel(); Conn conn = (Conn) key.attachment(); if (key.isReadable() && ch.read(conn.buf) < 0) conn.eof = true; conn.buf.flip(); if (conn.buf.hasRemaining()) ch.write(conn.buf); conn.buf.compact(); boolean pending = conn.buf.position() > 0; if (conn.eof && !pending) { ch.close(); return; } int ops = 0; if (!conn.eof && conn.buf.hasRemaining()) ops |= SelectionKey.OP_READ; if (pending) ops |= SelectionKey.OP_WRITE; key.interestOps(ops); } // busy spin: OP_WRITE only if pending // backpressure: OP_READ only if the buffer has room

alt.html: private fun serve(key: SelectionKey) { val ch = key.channel() as SocketChannel val conn = key.attachment() as Conn if (key.isReadable && ch.read(conn.buf) < 0) conn.eof = true conn.buf.flip() if (conn.buf.hasRemaining()) ch.write(conn.buf) conn.buf.compact() val pending = conn.buf.position() > 0 if (conn.eof && !pending) { ch.close(); return } var ops = 0 if (!conn.eof && conn.buf.hasRemaining()) ops = ops or SelectionKey.OP_READ if (pending) ops = ops or SelectionKey.OP_WRITE key.interestOps(ops) } // busy spin: OP_WRITE only if pending // backpressure: OP_READ only if the buffer has room

recap: A ByteBuffer has position, limit and capacity. flip() switches to reading, compact() keeps unread bytes and switches back, clear() forgets everything.
A non-blocking read returns what is there (maybe 0, or -1 at EOF), and write may send only part of the buffer. Keep unsent bytes per connection.
One read is not one message. Frame your protocol with a delimiter or a length prefix.
Remove every handled key from selectedKeys(). One thread owns a selector and does all the work for its channels.
Linux selectors are level-triggered epoll, so OP_WRITE on an idle socket fires forever. Arm it only while bytes are pending, drop OP_READ while your buffer is full, and close only when drained.
The limit: all of this bookkeeping is yours, and one slow step in serve holds up every connection on the selector's thread.

explain.prompt: Explain to a friend why an NIO echo server must not keep OP_WRITE registered all the time, and what it should do after a write that sent only part of its buffer.
explain.answer: On Linux the selector is level-triggered: it reports a channel for as long as the condition holds, like a light that stays on. A socket is writable whenever its send buffer has room, which is almost always, so a permanent OP_WRITE makes every select() return at once and the loop burns a core doing nothing. After a partial write, the server should keep the unsent bytes (call compact() so they move to the front), register OP_WRITE so the selector says when the socket can take more, and go back to select() to serve other connections. When a later write drains the buffer, it removes OP_WRITE again. While the buffer is full it should also drop OP_READ, which pushes back on a client that sends faster than it reads.

deeper.html:
Level-triggered and edge-triggered are the two ways epoll can report readiness. Level-triggered, the default, reports a socket on every epoll_wait for as long as it is readable or writable: the light that stays on. Edge-triggered (EPOLLET) reports it once, when it changes from not ready to ready, and then stays quiet until the next change: the bell. The JDK's EPollSelectorImpl never sets EPOLLET, so Selector is level-triggered on Linux. That is forgiving for reads (leave bytes unread, and the next select() tells you again) and unforgiving for OP_WRITE.

Edge-triggered code has the opposite trap: after a notification you must read until read returns 0, or you never hear about the leftover bytes. The JDK's virtual-thread poller, which lesson 8 looks at, uses a third mode, EPOLLONESHOT: report once, then disarm until the socket is registered again. That fits its job, which is to wake one parked thread once.

Two more details from the JDK source. EPollSelectorImpl asks epoll_wait for at most min(fdLimit, 1024) events per call, so a selector with 10,000 ready sockets needs several calls to see them all. And Netty's NIO transport still carries a guard against selectors that return early with nothing selected: after 512 such returns in a row (io.netty.selectorAutoRebuildThreshold), it rebuilds the selector. That is the workaround for the old "epoll spin bug", and the reason Netty counts empty wakeups.

To see the system calls yourself on Linux, run any demo that uses only JDK classes outside Gradle with strace -f -c -e trace=epoll_wait,epoll_ctl java -cp nio/build/classes/java/demo <class>. -c prints a count per system call when the program exits.
